janson-problem-18-39-condensation-rate-r.why: The setup, the problem description, the rate (1), its two calibration checks, and the 'not a solution / not an equivalence' framing all match the record. The fix is about strength in two directions. (a) The draft leaves out the record's central claimed result, the conditional Proposition (with its quantifiers: every C, conclusion epsilon=(lambda-nu)/2 along n_j=a_j/(lambda-nu)), and calls the conditional argument 'unresolved', although the record presents it as proved and author-checked. (b) The record gives no proof of that Proposition. It points only to an analogous step in a companion memo for Problem 18.40. Its only derivation is the heuristic rate (1), which holds 'up to the bulk's own fluctuation' with an o(M) error. That error is far coarser than the scale the Proposition needs, since gap*M is about C*sqrt(a_j). So the record asserts the conditional but does not establish it. The entry should state it as asserted and author-checked, give no proof, and flag the gap, rather than omit it or upgrade it. The record also says the Question is 'equivalent, given the Proposition'. Its own text supports only one direction ('no' yields just a candidate counterexample). The Question also uses a different normalisation, [log pi_a + log a]/a, which drops the a-independent constant log(1/(lambda-nu))+1. And its fixed threshold a_j^(-1/2) is weaker than the Proposition's 'every C'. So an affirmative answer to the Question as worded does not directly meet the Proposition's hypothesis. The draft rightly avoids 'equivalence' and should say why. Minor: the problem should record Janson's conjecture, including the stronger subsequence form, not only the question.
janson-problem-18-39-condensation-rate-r.statement: [campaign result 2026-09-14, author_checked; reduction plus asserted conditional, not a solution] Svante Janson's Problem 18.39 in Simply generated trees, conditioned Galton-Watson trees, random allocations and condensation, Probability Surveys 9 (2012), arXiv:1112.0510, asks whether Y_(1)/n -> 0 in probability is possible in the condensation regime 0 < nu < lambda. Janson conjectures that it is not possible for the full sequence and, more strongly, that there are always epsilon > 0 and a subsequence along which Y_(1) >= epsilon n w.h.p. (Example 18.36 gives Y_(1)/n -> 0 in probability along a subsequence.) Setting: let w_k >= 0 with w_0 > 0, let Phi(z) = sum_k w_k z^k have radius rho in (0,infinity) with Phi(rho) < infinity, and put pi_k = w_k rho^k/Phi(rho), a law with generating-function radius one and finite mean nu > 0. Let m_n/n -> lambda > nu. (Y_1,...,Y_n) is n i.i.d. pi variables conditioned on sum m_n, Y_(1) = max_i Y_i, and M = (lambda-nu)n. Heuristic rate: carrying M in r = M/a boxes of size a has class weight binomial(n,r) pi_a^r up to the bulk's fluctuation, giving log P = M Lambda(a) + o(M) with Lambda(a) = [log pi_a + log(a/(lambda-nu)) + 1]/a. For pi_k ~ c k^(-beta) and for pi_a = exp(-a^gamma), 0<gamma<1, Lambda increases on large a, so the optimum is a = M (one box), matching the known condensation picture. Since limsup_a Lambda(a) = 0 and Lambda < 0 for large a, Lambda has infinitely many upper records a_1 < a_2 < ... (Lambda(a_j) > Lambda(a) for all a < a_j). The record asserts, as author-checked and with no proof given beyond reference to an analogous step for Problem 18.40 in a companion memo, the following Proposition: if for some epsilon > 0 and every C, along infinitely many records, Lambda(a_j) - max_{a <= epsilon a_j} Lambda(a) > C a_j^(-1/2), then along n_j = a_j/(lambda-nu), P(Y_(1) >= ((lambda-nu)/2) n_j) -> 1, so the conjecture holds. Caveat: the only derivation offered is the heuristic rate with an o(M) error, which is coarser than the order sqrt(a_j) resolution this hypothesis requires, so the record does not establish the Proposition. The record poses the open Question whether, for every law pi on Z_{>=0} with radius one and finite mean, [log pi_a + log a]/a has infinitely many records with gap exceeding a_j^(-1/2) below max_{a <= epsilon a_j} for some fixed epsilon > 0. This is not a proved equivalence with the conjecture. A negative answer would only give a candidate counterexample, still requiring proof that the allocation spreads. The Question's normalisation and fixed threshold also differ from the Proposition's hypothesis. The problem remains open. This is an unrefereed campaign result.
